pos: n. phrase (unfermented or newly fermenting wine; the figure of the new covenant's power against old forms)
etymology: The Greek oinos neos is wine newly made and still working; the old bottles are skins, already stretched once and unable to give again.
biblical_def: “Neither do men put new wine into old bottles: else the bottles break, and the wine runneth out, and the bottles perish: but they put new wine into new bottles, and both are preserved” (Mat 9:17; Mar 2:22; Luk 5:37–38). The saying answers a question about fasting, and is paired with the patch of new cloth on an old garment. At the Supper the Lord promises a future drinking: “I will not drink henceforth of this fruit of the vine, until that day when I drink it new with you in my Father's kingdom” (Mat 26:29). At Pentecost the mockers said, “These men are full of new wine” (Act 2:13).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines wine as the fermented juice of grapes; and must as new wine, wine pressed from the grape but not fermented.
webster_full: WINE, n. The fermented juice of grapes.
2. The juice of certain fruits, prepared with sugar, spirits, &c.
MUST, n. New wine; wine pressed from the grape but not fermented.
scriptures: Mat 9:17
Neither do men put new wine into old bottles: else the bottles break, and the wine runneth out, and the bottles perish: but they put new wine into new bottles, and both are preserved.
Mar 2:22
And no man putteth new wine into old bottles: else the new wine doth burst the bottles, and the wine is spilled, and the bottles will be marred: but new wine must be put into new bottles.
But I say unto you, I will not drink henceforth of this fruit of the vine, until that day when I drink it new with you in my Father's kingdom.
Act 2:13
Others mocking said, These men are full of new wine.
Luk 5:39
No man also having drunk old wine straightway desireth new: for he saith, The old is better.
corruption_summary: The saying is quoted for novelty in worship, and it is about the covenant, not about the furniture.
corruption_paragraphs: New wine in old bottles has become the standard proof-text for changing whatever a congregation finds tired — the music, the order, the hour, the building — with the tradition cast as the brittle old skin. The Lord was answering a question about fasting, put by John's disciples, and the new wine is the arrival of the bridegroom and the covenant He brings; the old bottles are the whole apparatus of the ceremonial law and the Pharisaic additions to it, which could not contain what had come. That is a statement about redemptive history, not a licence to redecorate, and using it for the second cheapens the first.

Luke adds a line the other two omit and it cuts against the novelty reading entirely: “No man also having drunk old wine straightway desireth new: for he saith, The old is better” (Luk 5:39). The Lord is not commending appetite for the new as such; He is observing, with some sadness, why men would not receive Him — they had drunk the old and preferred it. A church that quotes verse 37 and never verse 39 has taken half a paragraph.

Acts 2:13 is the phrase in the mouth of scoffers, and it is worth noticing what looked like drunkenness: men speaking the wonderful works of God in the languages of the nations present. The charge was false and it was not baseless — something was happening that respectable religion had no category for. A church so orderly that no one could conceivably mistake it for anything, and a church so disorderly that the mistake is reasonable, have each got hold of one end of that verse.
roots_summary: Greek oinos neos (G3631, G3501), new wine; askos (G779), a wineskin, bottle; gleukos (G1098), sweet or new wine; Hebrew tirosh (H8492), new wine.
roots_lines: Greek oinos neos (G3631 with G3501) — new wine; Matthew 9:17, Mark 2:22, Luke 5:37–38.
Greek askos (G779) — a leathern bottle, wineskin; Matthew 9:17, Mark 2:22, Luke 5:37–38 only.
Greek gleukos (G1098) — new, sweet wine; Acts 2:13 only; Hebrew tirosh (H8492), Proverbs 3:10, Joel 2:24.
usage: “New wine into old bottles” — an answer about fasting, not furniture.
“The old is better” — the line the novelty reading omits.
“These men are full of new wine” — a false charge that was not baseless.

pos: n. (the shovel or fan used to toss threshed grain into the wind; the Authorized Version calls it a fan)
etymology: To winnow is to expose to the wind, from Old English windwian. The Authorized Version's word is fan, Greek ptuon; winnowing fork is the rendering of later versions.
biblical_def: John the Baptist of the coming One: “Whose fan is in his hand, and he will throughly purge his floor, and gather his wheat into the garner; but he will burn up the chaff with unquenchable fire” (Mat 3:12; Luk 3:17). The threshing-floor and the wind are the standing figure of separation: the ungodly “are like the chaff which the wind driveth away” (Psa 1:4); “I will fan them with a fan in the gates of the land” (Jer 15:7). Boaz “winnoweth barley to night in the threshingfloor” (Rut 3:2).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines fan as an instrument for winnowing grain; and to winnow as to separate and drive off the chaff from grain by means of wind, or to examine, to sift for the purpose of separating the bad from the good.
webster_full: FAN, n. An instrument used by ladies to move the air and cool the face.
2. An instrument for winnowing grain.
WINNOW, v.t. To separate and drive off the chaff from grain by means of wind.
2. To examine; to sift for the purpose of separating the bad from the good.
scriptures: Mat 3:12
Whose fan is in his hand, and he will throughly purge his floor, and gather his wheat into the garner; but he will burn up the chaff with unquenchable fire.
Luk 3:17
Whose fan is in his hand, and he will throughly purge his floor, and will gather the wheat into his garner; but the chaff he will burn with fire unquenchable.
Psa 1:4
The ungodly are not so: but are like the chaff which the wind driveth away.
Jer 15:7
And I will fan them with a fan in the gates of the land; I will bereave them of children, I will destroy my people, since they return not from their ways.
Rut 3:2
And now is not Boaz of our kindred, with whose maidens thou wast? Behold, he winnoweth barley to night in the threshingfloor.
corruption_summary: The gentle Baptist of popular imagination is the man who introduced Christ with a fire that is not quenched.
corruption_paragraphs: The title of this entry is worth a note, since the Authorized Version says fan and later versions say winnowing fork or winnowing shovel. All three render ptuon, the flat wooden implement used to throw threshed grain into the evening wind so that the chaff blows off and the wheat falls back on the floor. The AV's word is not archaic carelessness; a fan is a thing that moves air, and the older English was exact. Readers who meet the phrase in one version and the other should know they are looking at one tool.

The image's force is that it is John's introduction of the Messiah. Before there is a Sermon on the Mount, before a single healing, the forerunner announces One whose fan is in His hand, who will thoroughly purge His floor, and who will burn the chaff with fire unquenchable. The wheat and the chaff have been lying together on the same floor, indistinguishable to anyone walking past; the fan does not create the difference but reveals it, which is what judgment does. A gospel presentation that cannot contain John's sentence has edited the man God sent to prepare the way.

Psalm 1 supplies the reason the chaff cannot survive the wind: it has no weight. The ungodly are not described as strong opponents but as light — nothing in them to hold them down when the air moves — and the whole psalm's contrast is between a tree with roots by the water and husks. That is a more searching diagnosis than wickedness, and it is why the judgment in the figure needs no violence. It only needs wind.
roots_summary: Greek ptuon (G4425), a winnowing fan; diakatharizo (G1245), to cleanse thoroughly; achuron (G892), chaff; Hebrew mots (H4671), chaff; zarah (H2219), to scatter, winnow.
roots_lines: Greek ptuon (G4425) — fan, winnowing shovel; Matthew 3:12, Luke 3:17 only.
Greek achuron (G892) — chaff; Matthew 3:12, Luke 3:17; Hebrew mots (H4671), Psalm 1:4, Isaiah 17:13, Hosea 13:3.
Hebrew zarah (H2219) — to winnow, scatter; Jeremiah 15:7, Ruth 3:2, Isaiah 30:24.
usage: “Whose fan is in his hand” — the AV's word for the winnowing fork.
“He will throughly purge his floor” — the wheat and chaff had been lying together.
“Like the chaff which the wind driveth away” — the diagnosis is weightlessness.

pos: n. phrase (the wisdom that descends from God, distinguished by James from an earthly counterfeit)
etymology: James's phrase is he anothen sophia, the wisdom from above — the same adverb he uses of every good gift coming down from the Father of lights, and John of being born again from above.
biblical_def: “But the wisdom that is from above is first pure, then peaceable, gentle, and easy to be intreated, full of mercy and good fruits, without partiality, and without hypocrisy” (Jas 3:17). It is set against a counterfeit: “This wisdom descendeth not from above, but is earthly, sensual, devilish” (Jas 3:15), whose marks are bitter envying and strife. It is to be asked for: “If any of you lack wisdom, let him ask of God, that giveth to all men liberally, and upbraideth not; and it shall be given him” (Jas 1:5). Its beginning is fixed: “The fear of the LORD is the beginning of wisdom” (Pro 9:10), and its person is Christ, “who of God is made unto us wisdom” (1Co 1:30).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines wisdom as the right use or exercise of knowledge; the choice of laudable ends, and of the best means to accomplish them; and, in Scripture, true religion, godliness, piety, the knowledge and fear of God.
webster_full: WISDOM, n. The right use or exercise of knowledge; the choice of laudable ends, and of the best means to accomplish them.
2. In Scripture, human learning; erudition; knowledge of arts and sciences.
3. Quickness of intellect; readiness of apprehension; dexterity in execution.
4. Profound knowledge; and in theology, godliness, piety; the knowledge and fear of God, and sincere and uniform obedience to his commands.
scriptures: Jas 3:17
But the wisdom that is from above is first pure, then peaceable, gentle, and easy to be intreated, full of mercy and good fruits, without partiality, and without hypocrisy.
Jas 3:15
This wisdom descendeth not from above, but is earthly, sensual, devilish.
Jas 1:5
If any of you lack wisdom, let him ask of God, that giveth to all men liberally, and upbraideth not; and it shall be given him.
Pro 9:10
The fear of the LORD is the beginning of wisdom: and the knowledge of the holy is understanding.
But of him are ye in Christ Jesus, who of God is made unto us wisdom, and righteousness, and sanctification, and redemption:
corruption_summary: Wisdom is measured by cleverness, and James tests it by a list of behaviours with purity at the head and peaceableness second.
corruption_paragraphs: James 3:17 is a test, and its order is deliberate. The wisdom from above is first pure, then peaceable — purity before peace, so that a peace bought by compromise is disqualified at the first word; and then a run of qualities that are almost entirely about how a man behaves toward other people: gentle, easy to be intreated, full of mercy, without partiality, without hypocrisy. Not one of them is intellectual. A man may be right, learned and persuasive and fail every clause of the verse, and James's judgment on that combination is in the two verses before: bitter envying and strife, glorying and lying against the truth.

The counterfeit is described with a startling word. This wisdom “descendeth not from above, but is earthly, sensual, devilish” — three steps down, and the last is demonic. James is not describing folly or ignorance; he is describing a real capability, effective in argument and in church politics, which has a source. Any Christian who has watched a doctrinally sound man dismantle a congregation has seen it work.

The remedy in the letter is not study but asking: if any of you lack wisdom, let him ask of God, that giveth to all men liberally, and upbraideth not. Two things in that promise are easy to pass over — God gives liberally, and He does not reproach the asker for having needed to ask. Most men who lack wisdom know it and expect the request to be met with a lecture, and the verse forestalls exactly that fear.
roots_summary: Greek sophia (G4678), wisdom; anothen (G509), from above; hagnos (G53), pure; eupeithes (G2138), easy to be intreated; daimoniodes (G1141), devilish.
roots_lines: Greek anothen (G509) — from above; James 1:17, 3:15, 3:17, John 3:3, 3:31, 19:11.
Greek eupeithes (G2138) — easy to be intreated, compliant; James 3:17 only.
Greek daimoniodes (G1141) — devilish; James 3:15 only; Hebrew chokmah (H2451), Proverbs 9:10.
usage: “First pure, then peaceable” — the order disqualifies a bought peace.
“Earthly, sensual, devilish” — three steps down, and it works.
“Giveth to all men liberally, and upbraideth not” — no lecture attached.

pos: n. phrase (the company of the faithful of Hebrews 11, surrounding the runner in chapter 12)
etymology: Greek nephos marturon. Nephos is a mass of cloud rather than a single one — a crowd so dense it has no countable edges; martus is a witness, whence martyr.
biblical_def: “Wherefore seeing we also are compassed about with so great a cloud of witnesses, let us lay aside every weight, and the sin which doth so easily beset us, and let us run with patience the race that is set before us, Looking unto Jesus the author and finisher of our faith” (Heb 12:1–2). The cloud is the company of chapter 11 — Abel, Enoch, Noah, Abraham, Sarah, Moses, Rahab, and those who were sawn asunder — of whom it is said that they “received not the promise: God having provided some better thing for us, that they without us should not be made perfect” (Heb 11:39–40).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines witness as testimony; attestation of a fact or event; that which furnishes evidence or proof; and a person who knows or sees any thing, and may be called to give testimony.
webster_full: WITNESS, n. Testimony; attestation of a fact or event.
2. That which furnishes evidence or proof.
3. A person who knows or sees any thing; one personally present.
4. One who sees the execution of an instrument, and subscribes it for the purpose of confirming its authenticity by his testimony.
scriptures: Heb 12:1

Wherefore seeing we also are compassed about with so great a cloud of witnesses, let us lay aside every weight, and the sin which doth so easily beset us, and let us run with patience the race that is set before us,
Heb 12:2
Looking unto Jesus the author and finisher of our faith; who for the joy that was set before him endured the cross, despising the shame, and is set down at the right hand of the throne of God.
And these all, having obtained a good report through faith, received not the promise:
God having provided some better thing for us, that they without us should not be made perfect.
Heb 12:3
For consider him that endured such contradiction of sinners against himself, lest ye be wearied and faint in your minds.
corruption_summary: The cloud is imagined as a crowd in a stadium watching us run, and the word means those who have testified rather than those who are spectating.
corruption_paragraphs: The popular picture has the saints of Hebrews 11 leaning over the rail of heaven, watching the Christian's race and cheering. It is a warm image and the text does not quite say it. Martus is one who bears witness, and the whole of chapter 11 is their testimony: by faith Abel offered, by faith Noah prepared, by faith Abraham obeyed. They are witnesses in the sense that they have given evidence, and the evidence is that this way of living is possible and that God keeps His word. Whether they also observe is not stated; what they do in the sentence is testify.

The chapter's last two verses are the ones that make the cloud remarkable, and they are almost never quoted with it. These all, having obtained a good report through faith, received not the promise — every name in the list died still waiting — God having provided some better thing for us, that they without us should not be made perfect. The heroes are not held up as men who got what they were promised; they are held up as men who did not, and kept going. That is why the exhortation that follows is to patience.

And the runner's eyes are directed away from the cloud in the very next clause: looking unto Jesus the author and finisher of our faith. The witnesses are around; the gaze is forward and upward. A devotional life spent studying the great figures of church history and not looking at Christ has the geometry of Hebrews 12 exactly wrong, and the chapter supplies the reason — He is the only one in the account who finished.
roots_summary: Greek nephos (G3509), a dense cloud, a throng; martus (G3144), a witness; ogkos (G3591), a weight, bulk; euperistatos (G2139), easily besetting; aphorao (G872), to look away unto.
roots_lines: Greek nephos (G3509) — a cloud, throng; Hebrews 12:1 only — a mass, not a single cloud.
Greek martus (G3144) — witness; Hebrews 12:1, Acts 1:8, Revelation 2:13, whence martyr.
Greek aphorao (G872) — to look away from other things unto; Hebrews 12:2, Philippians 2:23.
usage: “Compassed about with so great a cloud of witnesses” — those who testified, not spectators.
“These all… received not the promise” — the heroes died waiting.
“Looking unto Jesus” — the gaze is not on the cloud.

pos: n. phrase (the wife of Proverbs 31; Hebrew eshet chayil, a woman of strength or force)
etymology: Hebrew chayil is strength, army, wealth, might — the word used of a soldier's valour and a nation's forces. The Authorized Version renders eshet chayil as a virtuous woman, which is true and softer than the Hebrew.
biblical_def: “Who can find a virtuous woman? for her price is far above rubies” (Pro 31:10). The poem that follows is an acrostic describing a woman who buys a field, plants a vineyard, trades profitably, works in wool and flax, gives to the poor, is clothed with strength and honour, and opens her mouth with wisdom. Its verdict is not on any of that: “Favour is deceitful, and beauty is vain: but a woman that feareth the LORD, she shall be praised” (Pro 31:30). Boaz uses the same phrase of Ruth: “all the city of my people doth know that thou art a virtuous woman” (Rut 3:11), and Proverbs elsewhere: “A virtuous woman is a crown to her husband” (Pro 12:4).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines virtuous as morally good; acting in conformity to the moral law; and, applied to women, chaste; and valor as strength of mind in regard to danger, courage, prowess.
webster_full: VIRTUOUS, a. Morally good; acting in conformity to the moral law; practicing the moral duties, and abstaining from vice.
2. Being in conformity to the moral or divine law.
3. Chaste; applied to women.
VALOR, n. Strength of mind in regard to danger; that quality which enables a man to encounter danger with firmness; personal bravery; courage; prowess.
scriptures: Who can find a virtuous woman? for her price is far above rubies.
Favour is deceitful, and beauty is vain: but a woman that feareth the LORD, she shall be praised.
Rut 3:11
And now, my daughter, fear not; I will do to thee all that thou requirest: for all the city of my people doth know that thou art a virtuous woman.
Pro 12:4
A virtuous woman is a crown to her husband: but she that maketh ashamed is as rottenness in his bones.
Strength and honour are her clothing; and she shall rejoice in time to come.
corruption_summary: Proverbs 31 is used to exhaust women with a checklist, and the poem is an alphabet of praise ending in the fear of the LORD.
corruption_paragraphs: The chapter is regularly preached as a specification, with the result that Christian women read the Bible's most extravagant compliment as a performance review. Two features of the text resist that. It is an acrostic — twenty-two verses running the Hebrew alphabet, a form used for praise and completeness rather than for instruction — and it is placed in the mouth of a mother teaching a king what to look for in a wife, not in the mouth of a husband telling a wife what to be. It is a portrait, and portraits are not schedules.

The Hebrew of the title is stronger than any English rendering. Chayil is the word for an army, for wealth, for might; it is used of mighty men of valour, and the same phrase applied to a man would be translated a mighty warrior. The AV's virtuous is accurate to the moral sense and loses the muscle. The woman of this poem buys real estate, runs a business, arms herself with strength, and laughs at the time to come; a reading that reduces her to domestic gentleness has translated the word down.

And the poem judges itself in verse 30. After twenty verses of competence — the merchandise, the candle burning at night, the tapestry, the fine linen sold to the merchant — the summary sets all of it aside: favour is deceitful, and beauty is vain, but a woman that feareth the LORD, she shall be praised. Every accomplishment listed can be counterfeited by a woman without the fear of God, and none of it is the ground of the praise. That is the same verdict the whole book of Proverbs gives on everything else, and it arrives, deliberately, on the last page.
roots_summary: Hebrew eshet chayil (H802, H2428), a woman of strength, force, valour; yare (H3372), to fear; oz (H5797), strength.
roots_lines: Hebrew chayil (H2428) — strength, army, wealth, valour; Proverbs 31:10, 12:4, Ruth 3:11; and of soldiers, Judges 6:12, 1 Samuel 16:18.
Hebrew oz (H5797) — strength; Proverbs 31:17, 31:25, “strength and honour are her clothing.”
Hebrew yirat YHWH (H3374) — the fear of the LORD; Proverbs 31:30, 1:7, 9:10.
usage: “Who can find a virtuous woman?” — the Hebrew word would be valour in a man.
“Strength and honour are her clothing” — the muscle the English softens.
“Favour is deceitful, and beauty is vain” — the poem setting its own list aside.

pos: n. phrase (Jeremiah's figure for the word of God as fire and as a hammer)
etymology: Jeremiah's two similes stand in one verse: fire, which consumes and cannot be held, and a hammer that breaks rock. Both are answers to prophets who were preaching dreams.
biblical_def: “Is not my word like as a fire? saith the LORD; and like a hammer that breaketh the rock in pieces?” (Jer 23:29) — spoken against prophets who said, I have dreamed. The prophet knows the fire personally: “then I said, I will not make mention of him, nor speak any more in his name. But his word was in mine heart as a burning fire shut up in my bones, and I was weary with forbearing, and I could not stay” (Jer 20:9). The Emmaus disciples felt the same heat: “Did not our heart burn within us, while he talked with us by the way, and while he opened to us the scriptures?” (Luk 24:32). Hebrews states it without figure: the word of God is “quick, and powerful, and sharper than any twoedged sword” (Heb 4:12).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines fire as heat and light emanating visibly from any body; and figuratively ardor of passion, vehemence, and the fire of the divine word; a hammer as an instrument for driving nails and beating metals.
webster_full: FIRE, n. Heat and light emanating visibly, perceptibly and simultaneously from any body.
2. The burning of fuel on a hearth, or in any other place.
3. Ardor of passion; vehemence; animation; as the fire of zeal.
HAMMER, n. An instrument for driving nails, beating metals, and the like.
scriptures: Is not my word like as a fire? saith the LORD; and like a hammer that breaketh the rock in pieces?
Jer 20:9

Then I said, I will not make mention of him, nor speak any more in his name. But his word was in mine heart as a burning fire shut up in my bones, and I was weary with forbearing, and I could not stay.
And they said one to another, Did not our heart burn within us, while he talked with us by the way, and while he opened to us the scriptures?
Heb 4:12

For the word of God is quick, and powerful, and sharper than any twoedged sword, piercing even to the dividing asunder of soul and spirit, and of the joints and marrow, and is a discerner of the thoughts and intents of the heart.
The prophet that hath a dream, let him tell a dream; and he that hath my word, let him speak my word faithfully. What is the chaff to the wheat? saith the LORD.
corruption_summary: The word's power is sought in the preacher's heat, and Jeremiah's fire is in the word whether the preacher is warm or not.
corruption_paragraphs: The verse before the figure sets up its point exactly: “The prophet that hath a dream, let him tell a dream; and he that hath my word, let him speak my word faithfully. What is the chaff to the wheat?” (Jer 23:28). The contrast is between men supplying their own material and men delivering God's, and the fire belongs to the second regardless of the temperature of the man carrying it. A preacher who tries to supply the heat himself has become one of the dreamers; his business is faithful delivery, and the burning is the word's property.

Jeremiah 20:9 is the other side and it is the loneliest verse in the prophets. He had resolved to stop — the mockery had become unbearable — and found he could not, because the word was a fire shut up in his bones and forbearing was worse than speaking. That is the experience of a genuine call, and it is nothing like enthusiasm; it is the inability to be quiet by a man who would very much prefer to be. Any minister deciding whether to continue should read the verse before he reads a survey.

The hammer is the half usually dropped, and it says something the fire does not. Fire consumes what will burn; a hammer works on what will not. The word deals with the combustible heart and with the rock, and both are broken, and neither is left as it was. Luke 24:32 is what it feels like when the fire does its work on a believer, and Acts 2:37 — pricked in their heart — is what the hammer feels like on a rock.
roots_summary: Hebrew esh (H784), fire; pattish (H6360), a hammer; dabar (H1697), word; Greek zon (G2198) and energes (G1756), quick and powerful.
roots_lines: Hebrew esh (H784) — fire; Jeremiah 23:29, 20:9, Deuteronomy 4:24, Hebrews 12:29.
Hebrew pattish (H6360) — hammer; Jeremiah 23:29, 50:23, Isaiah 41:7.
Greek energes (G1756) — powerful, active; Hebrews 4:12, 1 Corinthians 16:9, Philemon 1:6.
usage: “Is not my word like as a fire?… and like a hammer” — two tools, and the second is usually dropped.
“A burning fire shut up in my bones” — a man who wanted to stop and could not.
“What is the chaff to the wheat?” — the verse before the figure.

pos: n. phrase (the worship the Father seeks, as defined by Christ at Jacob's well)
etymology: The phrase is the Lord's own, given to a Samaritan woman who had raised the question of the right mountain; His answer moves worship off geography altogether.
biblical_def: “But the hour cometh, and now is, when the true worshippers shall worship the Father in spirit and in truth: for the Father seeketh such to worship him. God is a Spirit: and they that worship him must worship him in spirit and in truth” (John 4:23–24). The occasion is a dispute over place: “Our fathers worshipped in this mountain; and ye say, that in Jerusalem is the place where men ought to worship” (John 4:20), and the Lord answers that the hour cometh when neither will be the place (John 4:21). The truth in question is defined in the same Gospel: “Sanctify them through thy truth: thy word is truth” (John 17:17).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines worship as the act of paying divine honors to the Supreme Being; religious reverence and homage; and to worship as to adore, to pay divine honors to, to perform religious service.
webster_full: WORSHIP, n. Chiefly and eminently, the act of paying divine honors to the Supreme Being; or the reverence and homage paid to him in religious exercises.
2. The homage paid to idols or false gods.
3. Honor; respect; civil deference.
WORSHIP, v.t. To adore; to pay divine honors to; to reverence with supreme respect and veneration.
scriptures: John 4:23
But the hour cometh, and now is, when the true worshippers shall worship the Father in spirit and in truth: for the Father seeketh such to worship him.
John 4:24
God is a Spirit: and they that worship him must worship him in spirit and in truth.
John 4:20
Our fathers worshipped in this mountain; and ye say, that in Jerusalem is the place where men ought to worship.
John 4:21
Jesus saith unto her, Woman, believe me, the hour cometh, when ye shall neither in this mountain, nor yet at Jerusalem, worship the Father.
John 17:17
Sanctify them through thy truth: thy word is truth.
corruption_summary: In spirit is heard as sincerity or spontaneity, and in truth as personal authenticity, and the Lord meant the Holy Spirit and the Word.
corruption_paragraphs: The verse is the most quoted and least examined text on worship in the English-speaking church. In spirit has come to mean with feeling, from the heart, unscripted — so that liturgy is suspect and spontaneity is spiritual by definition. In truth has come to mean sincerely, authentically, as the real me. Neither is what the words carry. The contrast in the passage is not between formality and feeling but between two mountains: worship is being detached from a place, because the Spirit has come and the Word has been given, and those two are now what constitutes acceptable worship anywhere.

The Reformed have drawn from this the regulative principle — that God is to be worshipped as He has appointed in His Word and not otherwise — and the second half of the Lord's phrase is its warrant. If the truth is His word (John 17:17), then worship in truth is worship shaped by Scripture, and the question to ask of any element is not whether it moves the congregation but whether He asked for it. That is a stricter test than sincerity and a kinder one than taste, because it can be answered from a text rather than argued from preference.

The most striking clause is the one about the Father, and it is easy to read past: for the Father seeketh such to worship him. In a Gospel full of people seeking Jesus, this is the one place the seeking runs the other way, and its object is worshippers. Whatever else the verse settles about form, it says that God is not a reluctant recipient of worship who must be persuaded, but the one party in the transaction who is actively looking — and He found the first of them at a well, at noon, in a woman with five husbands.

pos: n. phrase (the consuming zeal of Psalm 69, applied to Christ at the cleansing of the temple)
etymology: Greek zelos, heat, fervour, jealousy for something. The psalm's verb is eat up — a zeal that consumes the man who has it.
biblical_def: “And his disciples remembered that it was written, The zeal of thine house hath eaten me up” (John 2:17), recalled as He drove out the money-changers with a scourge of small cords (John 2:15). The quotation is Psalm 69:9: “For the zeal of thine house hath eaten me up; and the reproaches of them that reproached thee are fallen upon me” — a psalm Paul also applies to Christ (Rom 15:3). The Lord's charge against the traders is Jeremiah's: “It is written, My house shall be called the house of prayer; but ye have made it a den of thieves” (Mat 21:13).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines zeal as passionate ardor in the pursuit of any thing; in general, ardor in the pursuit of good, or in the maintenance of a cause; and warns that it may be ill-directed.
webster_full: ZEAL, n. Passionate ardor in the pursuit of any thing. In general, zeal is an eagerness of desire to accomplish or obtain some object, and it may be manifested either in favor of any person or thing, or in opposition to it.
It is usually applied to religion or to some good cause, but it may be applied to a bad object.
ZEALOUS, a. Warmly engaged or ardent in the pursuit of an object.
scriptures: John 2:17
And his disciples remembered that it was written, The zeal of thine house hath eaten me up.
John 2:15
And when he had made a scourge of small cords, he drove them all out of the temple, and the sheep, and the oxen; and poured out the changers' money, and overthrew the tables;
Psa 69:9
For the zeal of thine house hath eaten me up; and the reproaches of them that reproached thee are fallen upon me.
And said unto them, It is written, My house shall be called the house of prayer; but ye have made it a den of thieves.
Rom 15:3
For even Christ pleased not himself; but, as it is written, The reproaches of them that reproached thee fell on me.
corruption_summary: The cleansing of the temple is borrowed to justify a temper, and the psalm says the zeal consumed the One who had it.
corruption_paragraphs: This is the passage angry Christians reach for, and the borrowing usually fails on three counts. The zeal is for God's house, not for the man's own honour — Christ was silent under personal insult and violent only about His Father's courts. It was deliberate rather than sudden: John says He made a scourge of small cords, which takes time, and Mark records that on an earlier visit He looked round about upon all things and, the hour being late, went out to Bethany and came back the next day. And the psalm's verb points inward: the zeal hath eaten me up. It consumed Him, and He paid for it; a temper that costs its owner nothing and its neighbours a good deal is not this.

The charge He brought is worth reading in full, because the modern application usually stops at the tables. My house shall be called the house of prayer — that is Isaiah, and Isaiah's sentence continues, for all people — but ye have made it a den of thieves. The market was in the court of the Gentiles, the one place a God-fearing foreigner could pray, and it had been filled with livestock and currency exchange. The zeal was for a house whose door had been blocked, and the people blocked out of it were the outsiders.

Psalm 69 is the psalm of the reproached righteous sufferer, quoted repeatedly of Christ — they gave me vinegar to drink, they hated me without a cause, the reproaches of them that reproached thee are fallen upon me. Zeal in that psalm is not an emotion but a position: standing where God's honour is being attacked and taking the blows meant for Him. That is what the disciples remembered when they watched Him with the cords, and it is why the memory is recorded not as an outburst but as a fulfilment.
